aspect: EXAMPLE - the typo on the residence permit
description: A misspelling on an immigration document is not a cosmetic problem: the document is the identity. Every subsequent record is created from it, so the error replicates into tax, health, banking and employment.
energy_note: Living under a spelling you never chose.

aspect: EXAMPLE - correcting it is treated as suspicious
description: Requesting a correction generates a change-of-name event in systems designed to flag exactly that - so fixing a clerk's typo can trigger the fraud checks that the typo itself never did.
energy_note: Punished for asking them to fix their mistake.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the credit file splits in two
description: Two spellings produce two thin credit files instead of one good one. The applicant appears to have no history, is refused, and cannot see why.
money_note: Higher rates, refused products, required deposits.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the credit file merges with a stranger
description: The opposite failure: fuzzy matching attaches another person's accounts or defaults to your file because the names are close enough. The burden of disproving someone else's debt falls on you.
energy_note: Refused a mortgage over a stranger's arrears.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the medical record that is not yours
description: Health systems match on name and date of birth. A split record means a missing history; a merged record means someone else's allergies, results and medications attached to your file.
energy_note: A clinical risk created by a spelling.

description: Tax authorities match name against the number. A mismatch rejects the filing, which can cascade into penalties, withheld refunds and a compliance record that later immigration applications ask about.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the background check comes back empty
description: A police or employment background check run against a misspelled name returns 'no record found', which is read not as clean but as unverifiable - and an unverifiable applicant is a rejected applicant.
energy_note: A clean record that cannot be found is worse than a bad one.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the child's surname does not match the parent's
description: Where a child's document was issued with a different romanisation from the parent's, proof of the relationship is questioned - at a school, a hospital, a border, or in a family reunification application.
energy_note: Asked to prove your own child is yours.

aspect: SCENARIO - two credit files, no credit
description: Omid's bank has him as OMID HOSEINI; his employer's payroll reports OMID HOSSEINI to the credit bureau. After three years of perfect payments he applies for a car loan and is told he has insufficient credit history. Both files are eighteen months thin. Neither is wrong.
money_note: Higher rate over the loan term, or refusal.
energy_note: Three years of good behaviour, split in half.

aspect: SCENARIO - the allergy that was not his
description: A hospital matches Omid to an existing record for an OMID HOSSEINI with the same birth year. The chart lists a penicillin allergy he does not have and omits the beta blocker he does take. He notices because a nurse reads it back to him. Nobody can tell him how long the records have been merged.
energy_note: A clinical near-miss produced by a spelling.

aspect: SCENARIO - proving his daughter is his
description: Omid's daughter is registered in Canada as SARA HOSSEINI. His own permit says HOSEINI. At a border crossing returning from Buffalo, an officer asks him to step aside and establish the relationship. He has no long-form birth certificate with him. It takes ninety minutes and his daughter cries.
energy_note: Asked to prove your child is yours, in front of her.
